question: A recent study of 862 European cities published in Nature Communications1 concluded that less than 15 % of the European population meets the basic criteria for daily access to urban nature using the 3-30-300 rule (tree visibility, tree canopy cover and proximity to parks). Furthermore, this study highlights a clear socio-economic gap, as higher income areas systematically have more urban green spaces.

Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 on nature restoration sets out the obligation to ensure that there is no net loss of green urban space or tree cover in cities by 2030, taking 2024 as the reference year. From 2031 onwards, these areas must increase, incorporating the integration of green areas into buildings and infrastructure. In view of the above: 1.
What measures is the Commission considering to ensure that inequalities in access to green areas between neighbourhoods are reduced in a verifiable manner?
Does the Commission intend to issue guidelines to prioritise investments in neighbourhoods with a greater deficit of urban green areas and prevent ‘green gentrification’?
Is the Commission considering establishing common access indicators to allow for comparable monitoring of cities?

Bertassello, L. E., van der Velde, M., Maes, J. et al., Assessing European cities with the 3-30-300 rule underscores the need for enhanced urban greening efforts, Nature Communications, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-71523-8 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) The Commission is not planning direct measures relating to addressing inequalities in access to green areas. However, the Nature Restoration Regulation1 will promote the greening of urban development in the future.

Moreover, the Commission has already produced guidance2 on how to develop urban greening plans as called upon by the Biodiversity Strategy3 for all cities with populations over 20 000. Such guidance strongly promotes working with citizens on developing a vision for cities and promotes addressing inequality.

No specific guidelines are planned in relation to investments in neighbourhoods with a greater deficit of urban green areas and to prevent ‘green gentrification’. However, the question of how and where to prioritise urban green space will be addressed in discussions on how to establish a ‘satisfactory level’ of green space under the post 2030 rules in the Nature Restoration Regulation.

As regards common access indicators to allow for comparable monitoring of cities, EU wide data is already publicly available on green space and tree cover in urban areas4. Furthermore, these data can be combined with population data by Member States or local authorities to study access to green space.

In addition, under the Green City Accord5, an EU initiative supporting cities committed to environmental improvement, signatories already report data on urban greenery using standardised indicators: percentage of protected natural areas on public land in a municipality and percentage of tree canopy cover within the municipality.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2024 on nature

restoration and amending Regulation (EU) 2022/869, OJ L, 2024/1991, 29.7.2024. 2 https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/bdb452c0-901c-11ef-a130-01aa75ed71a1/language-en. 3 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/biodiversity-strategy-2030_en. 4 https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/urban-atlas. 5 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/urban-environment/green-city-accord_en.
